l03.title: Lesson 3: Greetings, introductions and the weather

own-letters.title: å, ä and ö are letters of their own
own-letters.body: Swedish has 29 letters: the 26 of English, then å, ä and ö, in that order at the end of the alphabet. They are not a or o with marks, and a dictionary files them after z.

vowel-length.title: Long and short
vowel-length.body: A stressed syllable is long: either its vowel is long, or the vowel is short and the consonant after it is long. A double consonant in spelling marks the short vowel: tak /tɑːk/, tack /takː/. Length changes the vowel too: long a is /ɑː/ and short a is /a/, long u is /ʉː/ and short u is /ɵ/. The chart shows the nine long vowels.

sources.title: Engstrand (1990), Swedish, Journal of the IPA

sj-sound.title: The sj-sound /ɧ/
sj-sound.body: A voiceless sound made with the back of the tongue, lips slightly rounded. It is spelled sj, skj, stj, sk before e, i, y, ä or ö, and -ti- in words such as station.

tj-sound.title: The tj-sound /ɕ/
tj-sound.body: A soft voiceless hiss with the middle of the tongue raised, with no t in it. It is spelled tj, kj, and k before e, i, y, ä or ö: kjol, tjugo, köpa.

word-accent.title: Two word accents
word-accent.body: A word stressed on a syllable that another follows has one of two pitch patterns. Accent 1 is marked here with ̌ on the stressed vowel and accent 2 with ̂: anden /ˈǎndɛn/ "the duck", anden /ˈândɛn/ "the spirit". Most words of two syllables, and every compound, take accent 2. A word of one syllable has no contrast and no mark.

sources.title: Engstrand (1990), Swedish, Journal of the IPA

everyday-numbers.title: Numbers as they are said
everyday-numbers.body: The transcriptions give the careful forms. In everyday speech nio and tio are /ˈnîːɛ/ and /ˈtîːɛ/, and the tens drop their last vowel: trettio is /ˈtrɛ̂tːɪ/, fyrtio /ˈfœ̂ʈːɪ/. Hundra and tusen also come as etthundra and ettusen.

retroflex.title: r with t, d, n, s or l
retroflex.body: In Central Standard Swedish r merges with a following t, d, n, s or l into one sound made with the tip of the tongue raised just behind the gum ridge: ʈ, ɖ, ɳ, ʂ, ɭ. So fjorton is /ˈfjûːʈɔn/ and arton /ˈɑ̂ːʈɔn/, with no separate r.

gn-sound.title: gn is /ŋn/
gn-sound.body: After a vowel, gn is said /ŋn/, with the ng of English "sing": regn /rɛŋn/, lugn.

sources.title: Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen

igt-ending.title: The ending -igt
igt-ending.body: The g of -igt is silent: soligt /ˈsûːlɪt/, molnigt, blåsigt. The ending makes the form of an adjective that goes with ett-words, and with det in det är soligt, "it is sunny".

sources.title: Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen

en-ett.title: en-words and ett-words
en-ett.body: Every noun is an en-word or an ett-word, and the article says which: en lägenhet, ett hus. About three nouns in four are en-words. For most nouns there is no rule, so learn each one with its article; some endings decide it: nouns in -het and -ing are en-words (en lägenhet, en våning), and nouns in -um are ett-words (ett museum). A compound takes the gender of its last part: ett rum, so ett sovrum.

sources.title: Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen

definite.title: "The" is an ending
definite.body: Swedish says "the" at the end of the noun. An en-word adds -en, or -n after a vowel: lägenheten, trappan. An ett-word adds -et, or -t after a vowel: huset, köket. A short vowel keeps its long consonant, and spelling doubles it: rum, rummet. After i or på the definite form is usual where English says "the": i köket, in the kitchen.

sources.title: Lexin (Swedish–English), Institutet för språk och folkminnen
